title: Fasting across the church
hookLine: Orthodox Christians fast most Wednesdays and Fridays; Catholics fast in Lent; many Protestants fast for a cause

lines: A GREEK KITCHEN: BEANS, NO OIL.
A CATHOLIC KITCHEN: FISH IN LENT.
A BAPTIST COUPLE: NO LUNCH ALL WEEK.
cards: What's for dinner on a fast day? It depends whose kitchen you're in.
A Greek grandmother is cooking beans and greens in water, no meat, no cheese, no olive oil even, as she has on Wednesdays and Fridays for most of her life.

A Catholic family is having fish sticks, because it's a Friday in Lent. A young couple from a Baptist church have skipped lunch all week, joining their congregation in praying for a friend with cancer.
Very different menus. All of them would call it fasting.

teach.b: Start early. An ancient Christian handbook called the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays. Tradition links Friday with the day Jesus died, and Wednesday with the day he was betrayed.
That weekly rhythm is still alive.

Orthodox churches keep a long fasting calendar: on most Wednesdays and Fridays of the year, through Great Lent before Easter and in several other seasons, Orthodox Christians set aside meat and dairy, and often fish, wine and olive oil.

It's done in community, and people are told to adjust for health and circumstance. Catholic rules today center on a few days. On Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, adults fast: one full meal and two small ones.
On Fridays in Lent, no meat, which is why parish fish fries turn up in Lent. Giving up something personal for Lent is a familiar Catholic custom too.
Protestant churches vary widely. Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists often keep Lent; the early Methodists fasted on Fridays, and John Wesley urged it.
Some evangelical and Pentecostal churches call a fast for a specific need: a sick friend, a decision, a new year.
Some follow the pattern of Daniel, who said: "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth." The rules differ.
Underneath, each tradition is clearing something away, food, time, a habit, to make space: for prayer, for hunger to remind you, and for others.

how: Orthodox Christians fast from meat and dairy on most Wednesdays and Fridays and during several seasons; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and avoid meat on Lenten Fridays; many Protestants keep Lent or fast together for a particular need.

games.q: you're an early Christian reading the Didache. it says to fast twice a week. which days does it choose?
games.why: Wednesdays and Fridays. tradition links them to the betrayal and the crucifixion, and Orthodox Christians still keep them.

practice: Picture this month's calendar and pick one day on it, maybe a Wednesday or a Friday, the Didache's days.
Ask what you could fast from that day, meat, sugar, coffee, your phone after dinner, streaming, shopping, and choose one, noticing how it feels to decide in advance.
If you pray, offer that day to God now; if you don't, simply mark it as a day to make space.

wordCard.voice: Didache, an ancient Christian handbook that told believers to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, the start of a rhythm kept in many forms since.

carryVoice: Your line: make space. A calendar of fasts or none, the idea underneath is the same. Until tomorrow.
